# GeoTag Camera

> Free, open source, ad-free Android camera app that stamps photos with GPS location, address and timestamp. Built for field surveyors, students and NGO workers in India. Capturing, stamping and signing work offline, and each photo is signed on-device so it can later be checked for edits.

## Key facts

- Platform: Android 8.0 and newer (Kotlin, CameraX, Jetpack Compose)
- Current version: 1.2.0, published as a pre-release (not yet tested across many real phones)
- License: GNU GPLv3 or later
- Price: free, no ads, no subscriptions, no in-app purchases
- Data collection: none, no server, no analytics SDK, no ad SDK, no account
- Permissions used: camera, location (fine and coarse, only while the camera screen is visible); storage too, but only on Android 9 and older; internet only for the optional map and weather features
- Works offline: yes for capture, stamping, signing and verification; with no signal the stamp uses the nearest address cached on the phone, and the Plus Code is always calculated on the device
- Author: Konko Maji
- Source code: https://github.com/konkomaji/geotagcamera
- Downloads: https://github.com/konkomaji/geotagcamera/releases
- Website: https://konkomaji.github.io/geotagcamera/

## Core features (v1.2.0)

- Camera capture with GPS location, address and timestamp burned into the photo, with a live stamp preview in the viewfinder
- Two stamp styles: Bar (default), a full-width strip on the top or bottom edge with every enabled field (place and country code, address with Plus Code, coordinates, date and time with GMT offset, accuracy/altitude/bearing/weather chips, optional map thumbnail, organization logo and name, signed mark), and Minimal, a small coordinates-and-time label
- The stamp is moved by long-pressing and dragging it on the viewfinder; Bar snaps to the top or bottom edge, Minimal to one of nine positions
- Camera adapts to the phone: zoom presets from the real lens range, flash only when present, the phone maker's Auto/Night/HDR/Portrait/Retouch modes through CameraX Extensions when available, tap-to-focus with exposure compensation, pinch zoom, grid, front/back switch
- Aspect ratios 4:3, 16:9, 1:1 and Full; the saved photo is cropped to exactly the on-screen frame and stays upright with or without auto-rotate
- GPS position, altitude, accuracy, direction, capture time and time-zone offset written into the photo's EXIF metadata
- Photos saved straight to the phone's own Photos/Gallery app, nothing uploaded anywhere
- Gallery grouped by day with verified/edited badges, multi-select share and delete; photo detail can open the location in a maps app and copy coordinates
- User-selectable stamp fields with a live preview in Settings
- Custom organization or college name and logo on the stamp, free
- Tamper-evident photos: SHA-256 hash of the image pixels signed with an Android Keystore key generated on-device; the proof travels inside the photo, so any copy of the app can verify any photo, and the result shows the signing key's fingerprint
- Field-worker hand-drawn signature on the photo for inspection and muster-roll style records, optionally required
- Optional map thumbnail (Stadia Maps, OpenStreetMap data) and weather chip (Open-Meteo), both off by default; the map needs a build-time API key and is not available in the published APKs

## Who it's for

College students documenting fieldwork, land and infrastructure surveyors, NGO and government field staff, and anyone needing verifiable proof of where and when a photo was taken.

## Common questions

Q: Is it really free with no ads?
A: Yes, fully open source under GPLv3, no ads, no tracking, no subscription.

Q: Does it work without internet?
A: Yes. Taking, stamping, signing and verifying photos need no connection. Addresses come from the phone's built-in geocoder, which usually needs the network; with no signal the stamp uses the nearest address already cached on the phone, and the Plus Code always works.

Q: How is photo authenticity verified?
A: Each photo's image data is SHA-256 hashed and signed with a device-generated Android Keystore key at capture time, and the hash, signature and public key are embedded in the file. Verifying recomputes the hash and checks the signature. A pass means the pixels, including the burned-in stamp, have not changed since signing. The signature also covers the capture latitude, longitude and time, so rewriting the EXIF GPS or time fails verification; a copy with that metadata stripped shows "location not checked". It does not prove who signed the photo or that the GPS and clock were accurate.

Q: What leaves the phone?
A: Nothing goes to the developer. The optional weather chip sends the position rounded to about 1 km to Open-Meteo, the optional map downloads tiles from Stadia Maps, and the phone's own geocoder (usually Google Play services) looks up addresses. App data is excluded from cloud backup and device transfer.
